Recently, finding fault with aberrations in literary style, he further issued a special edict directing the responsible officials to correct them. This is what is meant by the Way combining…

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
君師身任斯文之責萬物所共快
覩焉者士生斯時其有弗與
於文者非夫也況兹土韓周
程朱之所寓遊也歐陸之所
產也而其流風又有存者乎
然則諸士子以文鳴
國家之盛宜然爲天下先有以
===
也雖然韓歐諸君子固皆有
功斯文然其所造或至或不
至是故一以詞章一以爲
理學優劣則𬨨別矣諸士子
於所嚮往可無擇乎必脩詞
立其誠反躬踐其實使蘊之
爲德行措之爲事業斯真無
punctuated:
君師，身任斯文之責，萬物所共快覩焉者。士生斯時，其有弗與於文者，非夫也。況兹土韓周程朱之所寓遊也，歐陸之所產也，而其流風又有存者乎？然則諸士子以文鳴國家之盛，宜然；爲天下先，有以也。

雖然，韓歐諸君子固皆有功斯文，然其所造或至或不至，是故一以詞章，一以爲理學，優劣則𬨨別矣。諸士子於所嚮往，可無擇乎？必脩詞立其誠，反躬踐其實，使蘊之爲德行，措之爲事業，斯真無
translation_en:
…ruler and teacher, personally shouldering responsibility for this cultural tradition—a sight that all creation rejoices to behold. A scholar born in this age who takes no part in this culture is no worthy man. Moreover, this land is where Han, Zhou, Cheng, and Zhu resided or traveled, and where Ou and Lu were born; does not their enduring influence still survive here? It is therefore fitting that its scholars should proclaim the flourishing of the state through their writing; there is good reason for them to lead all under Heaven.

Nevertheless, although Han, Ou, and the other gentlemen all contributed to this cultural tradition, some attained its fullest realization while others did not. Thus, one approach concerns literary composition, the other the learning of principle; their relative merits are distinctly different [?]. Can scholars fail to exercise judgment in choosing what they aspire to? They must refine their words to establish their sincerity, examine themselves, and put into practice the substance of what they profess, so that what they nurture within becomes virtuous conduct and what they apply outwardly becomes practical achievement. Then truly there would be no…

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
習於
聖教也已否則直藝焉耳豈所望
於今日哉〔偉〕不敏敢因成事
遂以勗焉茲舉也紀綱振作
使士不懈則有都察院右副
都御史秦〔鉞〕之昔任撫綏甄
陶長育使材有成則有巡撫
===
右副都御史胡〔岳〕之昔總方
嶽平定保釐使人樂學則有
右副都御史王〔浚〕之提督軍
務風勵褒嘉使吏知重則有
督木工部右侍郎兼右僉都
御史潘〔鑑〕及刑部郎中馮〔岳〕
工部員外郎陳〔垣〕戶部主事
punctuated:
習於聖教也已。否則，直藝焉耳，豈所望於今日哉？〔偉〕不敏，敢因成事，遂以勗焉。
茲舉也，紀綱振作，使士不懈，則有都察院右副都御史秦〔鉞〕之昔任；撫綏甄陶長育，使材有成，則有巡撫右副都御史胡〔岳〕之昔總方嶽；平定保釐，使人樂學，則有右副都御史王〔浚〕之提督軍務；風勵褒嘉，使吏知重，則有督木工部右侍郎兼右僉都御史潘〔鑑〕及刑部郎中馮〔岳〕、工部員外郎陳〔垣〕、戶部主事
translation_en:
…be versed in the teachings of the sages [?]. Otherwise, it would be mere literary skill: could that be what we hope for today? I, Wei, though lacking ability, venture to take the completion of this undertaking as an occasion to offer this encouragement.
For this examination, discipline was reinvigorated so that the scholars would not slacken: credit belongs to Qin Yue, formerly Right Vice Censor-in-chief of the Censorate. Through comforting and fostering, molding and nurturing, talent was brought to fruition: credit belongs to Grand Coordinator and Right Vice Censor-in-chief Hu Yue, who formerly exercised regional oversight. Through pacification and the maintenance of order, people were enabled to take pleasure in learning: credit belongs to Right Vice Censor-in-chief Wang Jun in his supervision of military affairs. Through encouragement, commendation, and praise, officials were made to recognize the importance of this undertaking: credit belongs to Pan Jian, Right Vice Minister of Works and concurrently Right Assistant Censor-in-chief, supervising timber procurement; Feng Yue, Bureau Director in the Ministry of Justice; Chen Yuan, Vice Director in the Ministry of Works; and the Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue …

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
〔□□〕行人龍〔逵〕先後以使事
監察御史兼有其勞綜理防
維小大咸飭則有右參政潘
〔漢〕尹〔嗣忠〕副使侯〔緘懷理〕
嚴〔州人〕左參議今遷副使戴
〔□〕雲南副使〔毛紹元〕右參議
任〔中〕僉事林〔應儒朱孔陽〕
周〔相〕方〔遠宜〕今遷參議趙〔業〕
都指揮李〔時謙〕而御史總
其凡云
福建建寧府儒學教授伍〔偉〕
謹序
punctuated:
〔□□〕、行人龍〔逵〕先後以使事，監察御史兼有其勞。綜理防維，小大咸飭，則有右參政潘〔漢〕、尹〔嗣忠〕，副使侯〔緘懷理〕、嚴〔州人〕，左參議今遷副使戴〔□〕，雲南副使〔毛紹元〕，右參議任〔中〕，僉事林〔應儒朱孔陽〕、周〔相〕、方〔遠宜〕，今遷參議趙〔業〕，都指揮李〔時謙〕，而御史總其凡云。
福建建寧府儒學教授伍〔偉〕謹序。
translation_en:
…[name illegible], and Messenger Long Kui, successively undertook official missions; the Investigating Censor also shared in these labors [?]. Those who coordinated affairs and maintained safeguards, ensuring that matters great and small were all properly ordered, included Right Administration Vice Commissioners Pan Han and Yin Sizhong; Surveillance Vice Commissioners Hou [Jian Huaili?] and Yan [the annotation reads “native of Zhou,” ?]; Left Administration Assistant Commissioner Dai [given name illegible], now promoted to Surveillance Vice Commissioner; Yunnan Surveillance Vice Commissioner Mao Shaoyuan; Right Administration Assistant Commissioner Ren Zhong; Surveillance Assistant Commissioners Lin Yingru, Zhu Kongyang [the two names appear together in one annotation, ?], Zhou Xiang, and Fang Yuanyi; Zhao Ye, now promoted to Administration Assistant Commissioner; and Regional Military Commissioner Li Shiqian. The Investigating Censor oversaw the whole undertaking.
Preface respectfully composed by Wu Wei, Professor of the Confucian School of Jianning Prefecture, Fujian.

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
嘗獨立鯉趨而過庭曰學詩乎對曰未也
不學詩無以言鯉退而學詩他日又獨
立鯉趨而過庭曰學禮乎對曰未也不
學禮無以立鯉退而學禮
知斯三者則知所以脩身知所以脩身則
知所以治人知所以治人則知所以治
天下國家矣
孟施舍之守氣又不如曾子之守約也
===
易
君子行此四德者故曰乾元亨利貞
益動而巽日進无疆
知變化之道者其知神之所爲乎
師者衆也衆必有所比故受之以比比者
比也比必有所畜故受之以小畜物畜
然後有禮故受之以履

第壹塲

四書

嘗獨立，鯉趨而過庭，曰：「學詩乎？」對曰：「未也。」「不學詩，無以言。」鯉退而學詩。他日，又獨立，鯉趨而過庭，曰：「學禮乎？」對曰：「未也。」「不學禮，無以立。」鯉退而學禮。

知斯三者，則知所以脩身；知所以脩身，則知所以治人；知所以治人，則知所以治天下國家矣。

孟施舍之守氣，又不如曾子之守約也。

易

君子行此四德者，故曰：「乾，元亨利貞。」

益，動而巽，日進无疆。

知變化之道者，其知神之所爲乎！

師者，衆也。衆必有所比，故受之以比。比者，比也。比必有所畜，故受之以小畜。物畜然後有禮，故受之以履。

書
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Once, he [Confucius] was standing alone when Li hurried across the courtyard. He asked, “Have you studied the Odes?” Li replied, “Not yet.” “Unless you study the Odes, you will have no means of expressing yourself.” Li withdrew and studied the Odes. On another day, he was again standing alone when Li hurried across the courtyard. He asked, “Have you studied ritual?” Li replied, “Not yet.” “Unless you study ritual, you will have no means of establishing yourself.” Li withdrew and studied ritual.

Knowing these three things, one knows how to cultivate oneself; knowing how to cultivate oneself, one knows how to govern others; knowing how to govern others, one knows how to govern all under Heaven, the states, and the families.

Meng Shishe’s maintenance of his vital force was nevertheless inferior to Zengzi’s holding fast to the essential principle.

Book of Changes

The gentleman puts these four virtues into practice. Thus it is said: “Qian: primal greatness, successful attainment, benefit, and correctness.”

Yi [Increase] is movement combined with compliance: daily advance without limit.

One who knows the way of change and transformation surely knows the workings of the numinous!

Shi [The Army] means a multitude. A multitude must have something with which to unite; hence Bi [Union] follows it. Bi means joining together. Where there is union, there must be some accumulation; hence Xiaoxu [Small Accumulation] follows it. Only after things have accumulated is there ritual; hence Lü [Treading] follows it.

Book of Documents

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
安民則惠黎民懷之
導沇水東流爲濟入于河溢爲滎東出于
陶丘北又東至于菏又東北會于汶又
北東入于海
其爾克紹乃辟于先王永綏民
凡人未見聖若不克見既見聖亦不克由
聖爾其戒哉爾惟風下民惟草
詩
樹之榛栗椅桐梓漆爰伐琴瑟
===
似續妣祖築室百堵西南其戶爰居爰處
爰笑爰語
王命召虎來旬來宣文武受命召公維翰
無曰予小子召公是似肇敏戎公用錫
爾祉
維女荆楚居國南鄉昔有成湯自彼氐羌
莫敢不來享莫敢不來王曰商是常
春秋
秋荆伐鄭公會齊人宋人救鄭〔莊公二十〕
punctuated:
安民則惠，黎民懷之。
導沇水，東流爲濟，入于河，溢爲滎，東出于陶丘北，又東至于菏，又東北會于汶，又北，東入于海。
其爾克紹乃辟于先王，永綏民。
凡人未見聖，若不克見；既見聖，亦不克由聖。爾其戒哉！爾惟風，下民惟草。
詩
樹之榛栗、椅桐梓漆，爰伐琴瑟。
似續妣祖，築室百堵，西南其戶。爰居爰處，爰笑爰語。
王命召虎：「來旬來宣。文武受命，召公維翰。無曰予小子，召公是似。肇敏戎公，用錫爾祉。」
維女荆楚，居國南鄉。昔有成湯，自彼氐羌，莫敢不來享，莫敢不來王，曰商是常。
春秋
秋，荆伐鄭，公會齊人、宋人救鄭。〔莊公二十〕
translation_en:
To bring peace to the people is benevolence; the common people cherish such a ruler.
He channeled the Yan River, which flows east as the Ji, enters the Yellow River, and overflows to form the Xing marsh. It emerges eastward to the north of Taoqiu, continues east to He, then northeast to join the Wen, then north, and finally east into the sea.
May you enable your sovereign to carry on the legacy of the former kings and bring lasting peace to the people.
Before people have seen a sage, they seem fearful that they will never see one; once they have seen a sage, they still cannot follow him. Take warning! You are the wind; the common people are the grass.
Book of Odes
Plant hazel and chestnut, yi trees, tong trees, catalpa and lacquer trees; in due course, fell them to make qin and se zithers.
Continuing the legacy of ancestral mothers and fathers, they build a dwelling with a hundred lengths of wall, its doors facing west and south. Here they dwell and remain; here they laugh and converse.
The king commanded Shao Hu: “Go forth to inspect and proclaim. When Kings Wen and Wu received the Mandate, the Duke of Shao was their mainstay. Do not say, ‘I am but a young man’; emulate the Duke of Shao. Begin diligently upon your great undertaking, and blessings will be bestowed upon you.”
You, Jing and Chu, dwell in the southern region of the realm. In former times, under Cheng Tang, even the Di and Qiang dared not fail to come with offerings, dared not fail to come and acknowledge him as king, saying, “Shang is the enduring rule.”
Spring and Autumn Annals
In autumn, Jing attacked Zheng. The duke joined men of Qi and Song to relieve Zheng. 〔Duke Zhuang, year twenty …〕

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
有八年　楚人伐鄭公子遂會晉人宋
人衛人許人救鄭〔文公九年〕
十有二月癸丑公會諸侯盟于薄釋宋公
〔僖公二十有一年〕
冬楚人陳侯蔡侯鄭伯許男圍宋〔僖公二
十有七年〕　六月公會宋公陳侯衛侯
鄭伯許男曹伯晉趙盾癸酉同盟于新
城〔文公十有四年〕　九月晉侯宋公衛
侯鄭伯曹伯會于扈〔宣公九年〕　夏叔
孫豹會晉趙武楚屈建蔡公孫歸生衛
石惡陳孔奐鄭良霄許人曹人于宋〔襄
公二十有七年〕
===
夏六月乙卯晉荀林父帥師及楚子戰于
邲晉師敗績〔宣公十有二年〕　吳伐我
〔哀公八年〕
禮記
君子齊戒處必掩身無躁止聲色毋或進
薄滋味毋致和節耆欲定心氣百官靜
punctuated:
有八年。楚人伐鄭，公子遂會晉人、宋人、衛人、許人救鄭〔文公九年〕。
十有二月癸丑，公會諸侯盟于薄，釋宋公〔僖公二十有一年〕。
冬，楚人、陳侯、蔡侯、鄭伯、許男圍宋〔僖公二十有七年〕。六月，公會宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯、晉趙盾，癸酉，同盟于新城〔文公十有四年〕。九月，晉侯、宋公、衛侯、鄭伯、曹伯會于扈〔宣公九年〕。夏，叔孫豹會晉趙武、楚屈建、蔡公孫歸生、衛石惡、陳孔奐、鄭良霄、許人、曹人于宋〔襄公二十有七年〕。
夏六月乙卯，晉荀林父帥師及楚子戰于邲，晉師敗績〔宣公十有二年〕。吳伐我〔哀公八年〕。
禮記
君子齊戒，處必掩身，無躁；止聲色，毋或進；薄滋味，毋致和；節耆欲，定心氣，百官靜
translation_en:
…the twenty-eighth year [of Duke Zhuang]. The men of Chu attacked Zheng. Gongzi Sui joined the men of Jin, Song, Wei, and Xu in coming to Zheng’s aid. 〔Ninth year of Duke Wen.〕
In the twelfth month, on guichou, the duke met the regional lords and concluded a covenant at Bo; they released the duke of Song. 〔Twenty-first year of Duke Xi.〕
In winter, the men of Chu, the marquises of Chen and Cai, the earl of Zheng, and the baron of Xu besieged Song. 〔Twenty-seventh year of Duke Xi.〕 In the sixth month, the duke met the duke of Song, the marquises of Chen and Wei, the earl of Zheng, the baron of Xu, the earl of Cao, and Zhao Dun of Jin. On guiyou, they jointly concluded a covenant at Xincheng. 〔Fourteenth year of Duke Wen.〕 In the ninth month, the marquis of Jin, the duke of Song, the marquis of Wei, and the earls of Zheng and Cao met at Hu. 〔Ninth year of Duke Xuan.〕 In summer, Shusun Bao met Zhao Wu of Jin, Qu Jian of Chu, Gongsun Guisheng of Cai, Shi E of Wei, Kong Huan of Chen, Liang Xiao of Zheng, and the men of Xu and Cao at Song. 〔Twenty-seventh year of Duke Xiang.〕
In summer, in the sixth month, on yimao, Xun Linfu of Jin led an army into battle against the viscount of Chu at Bi. The Jin army suffered a crushing defeat. 〔Twelfth year of Duke Xuan.〕 Wu attacked us [Lu]. 〔Eighth year of Duke Ai.〕
Book of Rites
When the gentleman observes ritual purification and abstinence, he must remain secluded in his dwelling and avoid agitation. He puts a stop to music and sensual attractions, allowing none to be presented. He takes plain food, without seeking perfectly blended flavors. He restrains his appetites and desires, settles his mind and vital energies, and keeps all his bodily faculties quiet…

translation_en:
…affairs, and impose no punishments, so as to secure what the quiet yin has brought to completion.

Heaven displays its signs, and the sage takes them as his model. The suburban sacrifice serves to make manifest the Way of Heaven.

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
功臣田土
乘輿服御物
孳生馬疋
盜賊捕限
第叁場
策五道
問書曰有典有則貽厥子孫詩曰貽厥孫
謀以燕翼子是帝王所以計久遠者在
教其子若孫而已洪惟我
===
太祖高皇帝深覽斯義建大本堂延四方名儒
敎
皇太子及
諸王又著
祖訓錄
儲君昭鑑錄以
賜至
太宗文皇帝命吏部翰林諸臣舉老成正大儒

punctuated:
功臣田土。
乘輿服御物。
孳生馬疋。
盜賊捕限。

第叁場
策五道

問：書曰：「有典有則，貽厥子孫。」詩曰：「貽厥孫謀，以燕翼子。」是帝王所以計久遠者，在教其子若孫而已。洪惟我太祖高皇帝深覽斯義，建大本堂，延四方名儒，敎皇太子及諸王，又著《祖訓錄》《儲君昭鑑錄》以賜。至太宗文皇帝，命吏部、翰林諸臣舉老成正大儒者傳
translation_en:
Lands belonging to meritorious officials.
Objects for the emperor’s clothing and personal use.
The breeding of horses.
Time limits for apprehending robbers and thieves.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions

Question: The Book of Documents says, “There are statutes and rules to be bequeathed to one’s descendants.” The Book of Odes says, “Bequeath plans to your descendants, thereby bringing peace to and protecting your children.” Thus, the means by which emperors and kings plan for the distant future lie simply in educating their sons and grandsons. Our august Emperor Taizu Gao deeply understood this principle. He established the Dabentang, the Hall of the Great Foundation, and invited renowned Confucian scholars from all regions to teach the imperial heir apparent and the princes. He also composed the Record of Ancestral Instructions and the Record of Illuminating Examples for the Heir Apparent to bestow upon them. When the reign of Emperor Taizong Wen came, he commanded the officials of the Ministry of Personnel and the Hanlin Academy to recommend mature, experienced, upright Confucian scholars to serve as tutors [?] …

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
皇太孫輯
文華寶鑑
聖學心法賜
皇太子其爲教詳矣顧於
東宮不設府僚以廷臣兼領其職何歟抑有
所祖述歟古之教太子必遠庖厨所以
長恩明有仁也而我
太祖高皇帝乃諭輔臣教
皇太子以兵事
===
太宗文皇帝北伐復俾
皇太孫侍行何歟抑有所取法歟昔漢臣賈
誼言太子之善在於早諭教與選左右
三代所以長久以有此具也然三代之
政具於書周之法尤莫詳於周禮顧於
教太子者無聞焉何歟漢唐宋東宮官
屬漸多亦多製述以示訓戒其治效反
不古若又何歟豈所謂善在太子師傅
之教固不足恃歟抑帝王所謂典則燕
punctuated: 皇太孫，輯《文華寶鑑》《聖學心法》賜皇太子，其爲教詳矣。顧於東宮不設府僚，以廷臣兼領其職，何歟？抑有所祖述歟？古之教太子，必遠庖厨，所以長恩明有仁也。而我太祖高皇帝乃諭輔臣教皇太子以兵事，太宗文皇帝北伐，復俾皇太孫侍行，何歟？抑有所取法歟？昔漢臣賈誼言太子之善在於早諭教與選左右，三代所以長久，以有此具也。然三代之政具於《書》，周之法尤莫詳於《周禮》，顧於教太子者無聞焉，何歟？漢唐宋東宮官屬漸多，亦多製述以示訓戒，其治效反不古若，又何歟？豈所謂善在太子師傅之教，固不足恃歟？抑帝王所謂典則燕
translation_en:
…the imperial grandson, and compiled the Precious Mirror of Literary Splendor (Wenhua baojian) and the Essential Methods of Sagely Learning (Shengxue xinfa) to bestow upon the crown prince. These provisions for instruction were indeed thorough. Yet why were no household officials appointed to the Eastern Palace, their duties instead being concurrently held by court officials? Was some earlier precedent being followed?

In antiquity, the crown prince’s education required that he be kept far from the kitchen, so as to foster kindness and manifest benevolence [?]. Yet our Emperor Taizu Gao instructed his assisting ministers to teach the crown prince military affairs; Emperor Taizong Wen, on his northern campaign, likewise had the imperial grandson accompany him. Why was this? Was there some precedent they took as their model?

Jia Yi, a minister of the Han, once said that the crown prince’s goodness depended upon instruction beginning early and upon the selection of his attendants. The Three Dynasties endured because they possessed these provisions. Yet although the government of the Three Dynasties is recorded in the Book of Documents, and nowhere are Zhou institutions set out more fully than in the Rites of Zhou, nothing is heard there concerning the education of the crown prince. Why is this?

Under the Han, Tang, and Song, the officials of the Eastern Palace gradually increased in number, and many works were also composed to convey instruction and admonition. Why, then, did the results of their governance fall short of antiquity? Could it be that the claim that the crown prince’s goodness depends upon the instruction of his preceptors and tutors is fundamentally unreliable? Or did what emperors and kings called standards and rules, and provision for…

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
冀者别有任也哉
皇上天錫祚胤本支日蕃發之之術蓋所欲聞
者諸士子咸懷忠愛之心將何以仰助
焉幸明告我
問仁統四端兼萬善故君子之學莫先焉
然道統之傳肇自堯舜乃獨言人心道
心而不及仁者何歟孔門之問答於仁
蓋數數矣乃猶謂子罕言仁者何歟子
思之學本諸孔子者也其書曰脩身以
===
道脩道以仁仁與道果二歟孟子之學
又得之子思者也其言曰仁者人也合
而言之道也仁與道果一歟嗣是諸儒
之說或以公言或以愛言或以覺言三
者果孰為近歟君夫統同合一之論將
安所歸歟今世以公言仁者未之聞矣
專□□愛則曰天地萬物為一體夫固
有所受也然其辭□惟使人含胡昏緩
無警切之意且或□認物為己而淪於
punctuated:
冀者，别有任也哉？皇上天錫祚胤，本支日蕃，發之之術，蓋所欲聞者。諸士子咸懷忠愛之心，將何以仰助焉？幸明告我。

問：仁統四端，兼萬善，故君子之學莫先焉。然道統之傳肇自堯舜，乃獨言人心、道心而不及仁者，何歟？孔門之問答於仁，蓋數數矣，乃猶謂「子罕言仁」者，何歟？子思之學本諸孔子者也，其書曰：「脩身以道，脩道以仁。」仁與道果二歟？孟子之學又得之子思者也，其言曰：「仁者，人也。合而言之，道也。」仁與道果一歟？嗣是諸儒之說，或以公言，或以愛言，或以覺言，三者果孰為近歟？君夫統同合一之論，將安所歸歟？今世以公言仁者，未之聞矣。專□□愛，則曰：「天地萬物為一體。」夫固有所受也，然其辭□惟使人含胡昏緩，無警切之意，且或□認物為己，而淪於
translation_en:
…for posterity have some other function [?]? Heaven has bestowed heirs upon His Majesty, and the principal and collateral branches of the imperial family grow daily more numerous. The means of developing them [?] are surely what he wishes to hear about. All you candidates cherish loyal and devoted hearts: how will you assist His Majesty in this? Kindly explain this clearly to me.

Question: Benevolence embraces the four beginnings of moral virtue and encompasses all goodness; thus nothing takes precedence over it in the gentleman’s learning. Yet the transmission of the succession of the Way began with Yao and Shun, who spoke only of the human mind and the mind of the Way, without mentioning benevolence. Why was this? Questions and answers concerning benevolence were certainly frequent in Confucius’s school; why, then, is it nevertheless said that “the Master seldom spoke of benevolence”? Zisi’s learning was rooted in Confucius. His book says: “Cultivate oneself through the Way; cultivate the Way through benevolence.” Are benevolence and the Way really two distinct things? Mengzi’s learning, in turn, derived from Zisi. He said: “Benevolence is being human. Taken together, this is the Way.” Are benevolence and the Way really one? Among the explanations of subsequent Confucian scholars, some speak in terms of impartiality, some in terms of love, and some in terms of awareness. Which of these three is truly closest? Where, then, should the argument that unifies them into one ultimately lead [?]? In our day, I have heard of no one explaining benevolence in terms of impartiality. Those who exclusively [two illegible characters] love say: “Heaven, earth, and the myriad things form one body.” This certainly has a received basis. Yet its wording [illegible character] makes people vague, muddled, and lax, without any sense of vigilance or urgency; moreover, some [illegible character] identify things as themselves and sink into…

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
秉受之矣專主夫覺則曰心有知覺之
謂仁夫亦有所受也然其弊不惟使人
張皇躁進無沉潛之味且或至認物為
理而昧夫精一之宗是其可無慎歟諸
士子相與究言之明以是之非趨聖傳
之正是主司所深望也
問大江以西士瘠民貧風氣為弱自滕王
分封以來雄文傑閣膾炙人口往往遂
為宗室之所托居世傳李氏出自唐裔
===
代有顯人今亦無以考其世矣迨夫宋
室南遷諸趙散處大都亦於茲土為盛
而其間名公哲人多由科目以進其立
身行事之畧時或載諸史志可考也以
今言之孝則有都監酒庫祖孫之相承
忠則有安吉南海後先之並著政事則
有心存爭而民稱趙母者有講學行
禮而士風翕然者文學則有延禮大儒
而潛心理學者有兩請漕舉而卓有詩
punctuated:
秉受之矣。專主夫覺，則曰：「心有知覺之謂仁。」夫亦有所受也。然其弊，不惟使人張皇躁進，無沉潛之味，且或至認物為理，而昧夫精一之宗，是其可無慎歟？諸士子相與究言之，明以是之非，趨聖傳之正，是主司所深望也。
問：大江以西，士瘠民貧，風氣為弱。自滕王分封以來，雄文傑閣，膾炙人口，往往遂為宗室之所托居。世傳李氏出自唐裔，代有顯人，今亦無以考其世矣。迨夫宋室南遷，諸趙散處，大都亦於茲土為盛。而其間名公哲人，多由科目以進，其立身行事之畧，時或載諸史志，可考也。以今言之，孝則有都監、酒庫祖孫之相承；忠則有安吉、南海後先之並著；政事則有心存爭而民稱趙母者，有講學行禮而士風翕然者；文學則有延禮大儒而潛心理學者，有兩請漕舉而卓有詩
translation_en:
…what is received at birth [?]. Those who give exclusive primacy to awareness say: “The mind’s capacity for knowing and perceiving is what is called benevolence.” This, too, has an inherited basis. Yet its harmful effects not only make people agitated and rashly eager to advance, without the savor of quiet, sustained reflection; they may even lead people to mistake things for principle and obscure the fundamental teaching of refinement and single-mindedness. Can one fail to exercise caution here? You candidates should investigate and discuss these matters together, clarify the rights and wrongs of these views, and turn toward the correct teaching transmitted by the sages. This is what the officials presiding over the examination earnestly hope for.
Question: West of the great Yangzi River, scholars are impoverished [?], the people are poor, and the prevailing spirit is weak. Ever since the Prince of Teng received his fief, magnificent writing and a splendid pavilion have been celebrated on everyone’s lips, and this region has repeatedly become a place where members of imperial lineages have made their homes. Tradition holds that the Li clan descended from the Tang imperial house and produced eminent men in successive generations, but their genealogy can no longer be verified. When the Song court moved south, members of the Zhao clan settled in scattered locations, with a particularly large concentration in this region. Among them, many distinguished gentlemen and wise men advanced through the examinations. Accounts of their personal conduct and deeds are sometimes recorded in histories and local gazetteers and can be consulted.
To speak of examples now: in filial piety, there were the grandfather and grandson, the military supervisor and the wine-depot official, who carried on the same tradition. In loyalty, there were the men associated with Anji and Nanhai, equally renowned in their respective times. In government, there was one who kept contention in mind [?] and whom the people called “Mother Zhao,” and another who lectured on learning and practiced ritual, bringing the scholars’ ethos into harmony. In literary learning, there was one who respectfully welcomed great Confucian scholars and devoted himself to the Learning of Principle, and another who twice sought nomination for the examination through the transport commission and was outstanding in poetry…

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
名者行誼則有善著庶能之稱而大儒
器之者有蚤聞忠義之訓而所立卓然
者清脩則有退居錦水二十年不磨勘
者有身爲帝胄而甘守布衣之操者俱
可得而言之歟至若身居宰輔文武忠
孝此固古今之所尊仰又不獨一鄉之
望而已而亦可獨舉而詳之歟我
祖宗封建法周親愛如舜唐宋不足言矣而其
爵封茲土者枝流蕃衍與
===
國同休不識於有宋諸賢之中亦或可取以
爲東平樂善之勸否也諸士子留心經
濟久矣茲非若輩所當尚論時邪
問五穀三幣之行世非不貴且便也惟以
其便也而輕用之則其勢不得不趨於
錢鈔矣且幣以利用宜矣彼錢者何爲
乎錢猶金之類可矣彼鈔者何爲乎歷
代之錢輕重不一而孰爲便而可行歟
鈔問
punctuated:
名者。行誼則有善著庶能之稱而大儒器之者，有蚤聞忠義之訓而所立卓然者。清脩則有退居錦水二十年不磨勘者，有身爲帝胄而甘守布衣之操者。俱可得而言之歟？至若身居宰輔，文武忠孝，此固古今之所尊仰，又不獨一鄉之望而已，而亦可獨舉而詳之歟？我祖宗封建法周，親愛如舜，唐宋不足言矣。而其爵封茲土者，枝流蕃衍，與國同休。不識於有宋諸賢之中，亦或可取以爲東平樂善之勸否也？諸士子留心經濟久矣，茲非若輩所當尚論時邪？

問：五穀三幣之行世，非不貴且便也。惟以其便也而輕用之，則其勢不得不趨於錢鈔矣。且幣以利用宜矣，彼錢者何爲乎？錢猶金之類可矣，彼鈔者何爲乎？歷代之錢輕重不一，而孰爲便而可行歟？鈔問
translation_en:
…a reputation for poetry. As for conduct and integrity, there were those whose goodness earned them a reputation for manifold abilities and whom great Confucian scholars esteemed, and those who heard lessons in loyalty and righteousness early in life and distinguished themselves by the principles they upheld. As for purity of conduct, there were those who retired to Jinshui and went twenty years without an evaluation for promotion, and those who, though descendants of emperors, willingly maintained the integrity of a commoner. Can all these men be identified and discussed? As for those who occupied the highest ministerial offices and displayed civil and military accomplishments, loyalty, and filial devotion, they have indeed been revered throughout the ages; their prestige extended far beyond a single locality. Can these men, too, be singled out and discussed in detail?

Our imperial ancestors modeled their enfeoffments upon the Zhou and loved their kin as Shun did; the Tang and Song do not merit comparison. The descendants of those granted noble fiefs in this region have branched out and multiplied, sharing in the dynasty’s blessings. Might examples from among the worthy men of the Song be selected to encourage a delight in goodness like that of the Prince of Dongping? You examination candidates have long devoted your attention to statecraft. Is this not the occasion for you to discuss the worthies of the past?

Question: The five grains and the three forms of currency circulating in the world are certainly valuable and convenient. Yet if, because of their convenience, they are used too freely, the tendency must inevitably be toward coin and paper currency. Moreover, it is fitting that currency should facilitate use, but what purpose does coin serve? Coin may be acceptable as something akin to gold, but what purpose does paper currency serve? Coins of successive dynasties have differed in weight: which are convenient and suitable for circulation? As for paper currency, [the following character is unclear in context: 問] …

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
時制也然亦有敝好不同而何能使之不壅
則或謂錢宜行於通都而不行於僻地
鈔宜行於草昧而不行於承平則今日
所爲論功議辟者無乃失實歟常聞先
王制錢義精而傳後世之鈔則鈔而已
亦有可言者歟方今
大
工告興國用爲絀急計則爲輸粟遠謀則有
發礦紙爲銀幣計耳而其間所得不補
其所亡者亦有之不知是二物者古昔
===
所以通變宜民之方而積於無用之地
顧猶以爲乏爲言何歟夫錢穀皆吾分
內而世務由於經術無曰明明求財利
者庶人之事也而忽諸
問救荒弭盜之策在爲政者均所當講而
江西尤急何者地狹人稠耕隊不足自
給一有水旱之災即其荒易見也深山
重湖藪澤藏匿一有萑苻之警即
其勢難靖也古之爲荒備者有平糴法
punctuated:
時制也，然亦有敝好不同，而何能使之不壅？則或謂錢宜行於通都，而不行於僻地；鈔宜行於草昧，而不行於承平。則今日所爲論功議辟者，無乃失實歟？常聞先王制錢，義精而傳；後世之鈔，則鈔而已，亦有可言者歟？方今大工告興，國用爲絀，急計則爲輸粟，遠謀則有發礦，紙爲銀幣計耳，而其間所得不補其所亡者亦有之。不知是二物者，古昔所以通變宜民之方，而積於無用之地，顧猶以爲乏爲言，何歟？夫錢穀皆吾分內，而世務由於經術，無曰明明求財利者庶人之事也，而忽諸。

問：救荒弭盜之策，在爲政者均所當講，而江西尤急。何者？地狹人稠，耕隊不足自給，一有水旱之災，即其荒易見也；深山重湖，藪澤藏匿，一有萑苻之警，即其勢難靖也。古之爲荒備者，有平糴法。
translation_en:
…a system of its time. Yet there are also differences in deterioration and quality [?]; how can its circulation be kept unobstructed? Some say that coins should circulate in major cities but not in remote places, and that paper money should circulate in times of founding disorder but not in settled peace. Are present discussions of merits and penalties [?], then, perhaps divorced from reality? We have often heard that the former kings’ principles for making coins were refined and handed down to posterity; the paper money of later ages, however, is merely paper money. Is there nevertheless something to be said for it?

Now that great construction works have been inaugurated and state finances are strained, the immediate expedient is to secure deliveries of grain, while the longer-term plan is to open mines—paper serving as silver currency is merely a financial expedient [?]. Yet in some instances the gains do not make up for the losses. These two things were the means by which people of antiquity adapted to changing circumstances and benefited the people. Why, then, are they allowed to accumulate where they serve no purpose, while people nevertheless speak of shortages? Money and grain both fall within our responsibilities, and the management of worldly affairs proceeds from learning in the Classics. Do not say that openly seeking material profit [?] is the business of commoners and therefore neglect these matters.

Question: Policies for relieving famine and suppressing banditry equally deserve the attention of those who govern, but they are especially urgent in Jiangxi. Why is this? The land is limited and the population dense; cultivation [?] does not suffice for self-support, so any flood or drought readily produces famine. Deep mountains, extensive lakes, and marshes provide hiding places, so once an alarm of banditry arises, the situation is difficult to pacify. Among the measures used in antiquity to prepare against famine was the system of purchasing grain at equitable prices…

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
有常平法有義倉社倉法其在昔者蓋
不無異議矣今將曷從爲盜備者有沈
命法有柎鼓法有義營懸賞法其行之
當時亦不能皆效矣今將安出或有爲
本末源流之論而推言禹湯受災不困
之因似乎釋諸法可盡廢也其信然歟
有爲舍本禁末之說而力沮熙寧盜賊
重法之請似沈命諸法可盡弛也抑確
論歟夫君子不恃患之未至恃吾有以
待之苟莫爲之所豈徒主司之憂亦二
三子生於其鄉者之羞也願詳言之
punctuated: 有常平法，有義倉社倉法。其在昔者，蓋不無異議矣，今將曷從？爲盜備者，有沈命法，有柎鼓法，有義營懸賞法。其行之當時，亦不能皆效矣，今將安出？或有爲本末源流之論，而推言禹湯受災不困之因，似乎釋諸法可盡廢也，其信然歟？有爲舍本禁末之說，而力沮熙寧盜賊重法之請，似沈命諸法可盡弛也，抑確論歟？夫君子不恃患之未至，恃吾有以待之。苟莫爲之所，豈徒主司之憂，亦二三子生於其鄉者之羞也。願詳言之。
translation_en:
…there are also the ever-normal granary system and the charitable and community granary systems. In the past, these were certainly not without their critics. Which should we follow today? Measures for guarding against banditry include the chenming law, imposing capital punishment for failures in suppressing bandits; the drum system [?]; and arrangements for volunteer encampments and the offering of rewards. Even when implemented in their own times, these measures did not all prove effective. What course should we now take?

Some discuss roots and branches, sources and downstream effects, and go on to explain why Yu and Tang suffered disasters without being reduced to distress. This seems to suggest that all these systems may be abandoned. Is that really so? Others argue that prohibiting secondary manifestations neglects the root, and vigorously oppose proposals for severe laws against banditry such as those of the Xining reign period. This seems to suggest that the chenming law and all such measures may be relaxed. Is this, then, a sound judgment?

The gentleman relies not on trouble having yet to arrive, but on having the means to meet it. If no provision is made, this is surely not only a concern for the officials responsible, but also a disgrace for you candidates, who were born in this region. Please explain your views in detail.

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
乎宜無不厚之恩聖人實無陰厚之教吾試舉
家庭所嘗聞者以告子焉是故退朝以燕退燕
以閒夫子蓋嘗獨立矣家有嚴君其可無禮鯉
之過庭而必恭敬以趨之也斯時也堂上惟父
堂下惟子欲有所厚此其可以厚矣夫子則問
以學詩乎而鯉以未也對之夫子則曰詩以聲
志而所由以言者不學則事理昧而心氣乖其
何以言鯉承夫子之教退而學詩本二南以求
其端也參列國以盡其變也正於雅以大其規
===
和於頌以要其止也必使涵泳從容而自得性
情之正言其寡尤乎然此特一事耳未足以盡
觀夫子也他日又嘗獨立矣雖見之狎夫敢不
貌鯉之過庭亦必齋栗以趨之也斯時也童蒙
匪求冀孝未侍欲有所厚此又可以厚矣夫子
則問以學禮乎而鯉復以未也對之夫子則曰
禮以治躬而所由以立者不學則品節踈而德
性蕩其何以立鯉服夫子之訓退而學禮忠信
以立其本也義理以考其文也求之實以□□
punctuated: 乎，宜無不厚之恩，聖人實無陰厚之教。吾試舉家庭所嘗聞者以告子焉。是故退朝以燕，退燕以閒，夫子蓋嘗獨立矣。家有嚴君，其可無禮？鯉之過庭，而必恭敬以趨之也。斯時也，堂上惟父，堂下惟子，欲有所厚，此其可以厚矣。夫子則問以「學詩乎？」而鯉以「未也」對之。夫子則曰：「詩以聲志，而所由以言者。不學則事理昧而心氣乖，其何以言？」鯉承夫子之教，退而學詩，本二南以求其端也，參列國以盡其變也，正於雅以大其規，和於頌以要其止也。必使涵泳從容，而自得性情之正，言其寡尤乎？然此特一事耳，未足以盡觀夫子也。他日又嘗獨立矣，雖見之狎，夫敢不貌？鯉之過庭，亦必齋栗以趨之也。斯時也，童蒙匪求，冀孝未侍，欲有所厚，此又可以厚矣。夫子則問以「學禮乎？」而鯉復以「未也」對之。夫子則曰：「禮以治躬，而所由以立者。不學則品節踈而德性蕩，其何以立？」鯉服夫子之訓，退而學禮，忠信以立其本也，義理以考其文也，求之實以□□
translation_en:
…surely his kindness should lack nothing in generosity; yet the sage truly gave no privately preferential instruction. Let me recount for you what I once heard within our household. Thus, after withdrawing from court to his private quarters, and then retiring to his leisure, the Master once stood alone. With an authoritative father in the household, how could one dispense with propriety? When I, Li, crossed the courtyard, I invariably hastened forward respectfully. At that moment, there was only the father above in the hall and only the son below. Had he wished to show special favor, this would have been an opportunity. The Master asked, “Have you studied the Book of Odes?” I replied, “Not yet.” The Master then said, “The Odes give voice to aspirations and provide the means of speaking. Without studying them, one remains ignorant of the principles of affairs, and one’s mind and vital energies fall into discord. How, then, could one speak?”

Receiving the Master’s instruction, I withdrew and studied the Odes. I took the Two Southern Sections as my foundation to seek their beginnings, consulted the Airs of the various states to encompass their variations, sought rectitude in the Elegantiae to enlarge my scope, and harmony in the Hymns to grasp their ultimate purport. Through unhurried immersion, I would assuredly come to attain for myself the proper disposition of human nature and feelings. Would my speech then not incur few faults? Yet this was only one incident, insufficient to reveal the Master fully.

On another day, he again stood alone. Though I saw him familiarly, how could I dare to neglect a respectful demeanor? As I crossed the courtyard, I again hastened forward with reverent apprehension. At that moment, no youthful learner was seeking instruction, and “Ji Xiao” was not in attendance [?]. Had he wished to show special favor, this too would have been an opportunity. The Master asked, “Have you studied ritual?” I again replied, “Not yet.” The Master then said, “Ritual governs one’s person and provides the means of establishing oneself. Without studying it, one’s standards of conduct become lax and one’s moral nature unrestrained. How, then, could one establish oneself?”

Accepting the Master’s instruction, I withdrew and studied ritual. Through conscientiousness and trustworthiness I established its foundation; through righteousness and principle I examined its forms; I sought it in actual practice in order to [two illegible characters] …

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
常協諸義以盡其變也必使闔成交錯而自無
易慢之入立其可與乎是則家庭所嘗聞者如
此然皆學者之所共聞也又何異焉夫子嘗曰
天有四時春秋冬夏風雨霜露無非教也地載
神氣神氣風霆風霆流形庶物露生無非教也
則夫子之教一天地也豈以父子而有所擇但
其教之之序則又視其所至何如耳是故顔之
四勿曾之一貫反為夫子之所獨厚而鯉則未
有聞也故陳亢無疑於聖人惟當求其獨厚
===
知斯三者則知所以脩身知所以脩身則
知所以治人知所以治人則知所以治
天下國家矣
張希舉
同考試官教諭鄧 批〔治天下國家處暗拾九〕
經而言最是
同考試官教諭唐 批〔脩身治人中以有若有〕
臣為政貫說得中庸之旨
同考試官教諭徐 批〔是題包含一章之旨場〕
punctuated:
常，協諸義以盡其變也。必使闔成交錯，而自無易慢之入，立其可與乎？是則家庭所嘗聞者如此，然皆學者之所共聞也，又何異焉？夫子嘗曰：「天有四時，春秋冬夏，風雨霜露，無非教也。地載神氣，神氣風霆，風霆流形，庶物露生，無非教也。」則夫子之教，一天地也，豈以父子而有所擇？但其教之之序，則又視其所至何如耳。是故顔之四勿，曾之一貫，反為夫子之所獨厚，而鯉則未有聞也。故陳亢無疑於聖人，惟當求其獨厚。

知斯三者，則知所以脩身；知所以脩身，則知所以治人；知所以治人，則知所以治天下國家矣。
張希舉

同考試官教諭鄧，批〔治天下國家處暗拾九〕經而言，最是。

同考試官教諭唐，批〔脩身治人中以有若有〕臣為政貫說，得中庸之旨。

同考試官教諭徐，批〔是題包含一章之旨，場〕
translation_en:
…constancy, coordinating these with righteousness to encompass every variation. One must ensure that all is brought to completion and interwoven [?], so that carelessness and disrespect find no entry. Might one then be able to stand firm? Such, then, were the teachings heard within the household; yet these were all teachings that students heard in common. What difference was there? The Master once said: “Heaven has its four seasons—spring, autumn, winter, and summer—and wind, rain, frost, and dew: none is without instruction. Earth bears spiritual forces; these become wind and thunder; wind and thunder give flowing form, and the myriad things emerge into life: none is without instruction.” The Master’s teaching thus accords with Heaven and Earth. How could he show preference on account of the bond between father and son? The sequence of his instruction, however, depended on the stage each learner had reached. Thus Yan’s four prohibitions and Zeng’s single unifying thread were, instead, teachings with which the Master especially favored them, whereas Li had not heard them. Chen Kang should therefore have no doubts about the sage, but should seek what it was in which he showed special favor.

“Knowing these three, one knows how to cultivate oneself; knowing how to cultivate oneself, one knows how to govern others; knowing how to govern others, one knows how to govern all under Heaven, the state, and the family.”
Zhang Xiju

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
中多財昂作獨得之
考試官教諭葉　批　此作卓有定見錄之
考試官教授伍　批　寫得題意出
君知所以立本則知所以爲政矣夫本立身
脩之謂也天下國家舉此而措之耳此夫子謂
文武之政所以有待於人存者也若曰爲政不
難脩身爲難吾前所以告君脩身者備矣君盍
知所以求之乎是故知仁勇天下之達德也而
即所以脩身之具也然學而非好不足以近智
===
行而非力不足以近仁耻而非知不足以近勇
故知斯三者則必好學也力行也知耻也而天
下之德不遠於心而得之矣由是知所以脩身
則必知及之仁守之勇强之而天下之道不遠
於身而得之矣夫君之所以立政者人也而其
所以取人者身也既知所以脩身則心純賢輔
而自有以來天下之章臣得化行而自可以舉
天下之廢關睢麟趾之意既不患於徒法而典
章文物之布又不患於徒善矣不知所以治人
punctuated:
中多財昂作，獨得之。

考試官教諭葉批：此作卓有定見，錄之。

考試官教授伍批：寫得題意出。

君知所以立本，則知所以爲政矣。夫本立，身脩之謂也。天下國家，舉此而措之耳。此夫子謂文武之政所以有待於人存者也。若曰：爲政不難，脩身爲難。吾前所以告君脩身者備矣，君盍知所以求之乎？是故知仁勇，天下之達德也，而即所以脩身之具也。然學而非好，不足以近智；行而非力，不足以近仁；耻而非知，不足以近勇。故知斯三者，則必好學也，力行也，知耻也，而天下之德不遠於心而得之矣。由是知所以脩身，則必知及之，仁守之，勇强之，而天下之道不遠於身而得之矣。夫君之所以立政者，人也；而其所以取人者，身也。既知所以脩身，則心純賢輔，而自有以來天下之章臣；得化行，而自可以舉天下之廢。關睢麟趾之意，既不患於徒法，而典章文物之布，又不患於徒善矣。不知所以治人
translation_en:
…Among the many compositions in the examination, [the wording 財昂 is doubtful: ?] this alone grasps it.

Examiner Ye, Instructor, comments: This composition displays exceptionally firm judgment. Include it in the record.

Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: It brings out the meaning of the topic.

When you, my lord, know how to establish the foundation, you will know how to govern. Establishing the foundation means cultivating oneself. Governing the realm, the state, and the family is simply a matter of taking this and putting it into practice. This is what the Master meant when he said that the government of Kings Wen and Wu depended on the presence of the right men. It is as though he said: Governing is not difficult; cultivating oneself is difficult. What I previously told you about cultivating yourself was comprehensive. Why do you not understand how to pursue it? Thus wisdom, benevolence, and courage are the universally applicable virtues of the world, and they are precisely the means of cultivating oneself. Yet learning without loving learning is insufficient to approach wisdom; acting without exertion is insufficient to approach benevolence; and shame without awareness is insufficient to approach courage. Thus, knowing these three means that one must love learning, act with vigor, and know shame. The virtues of the world will then be attained within the heart, without seeking them far away. From this, knowing how to cultivate oneself means that one must reach understanding through wisdom, preserve it through benevolence, and strengthen it through courage. The Way of the world will then be attained within oneself, without seeking it far away.

Those through whom you, my lord, establish government are other people; the means by which you select them is your own person. Once you know how to cultivate yourself, then your heart is pure and your assistants worthy [?], and you will naturally have the means to attract the illustrious ministers of the realm. Transforming influence takes effect [?], and you will naturally be able to revive all that has fallen into neglect throughout the realm. With the spirit of “The Ospreys” (Guan ju) and “The Qilin’s Hooves” (Lin zhi), there will be no concern that institutions are merely empty forms; and with the promulgation of statutes, institutions, and cultural observances, there will likewise be no concern that good intentions stand alone. Would you not know how to govern people …

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
□人之稱對已也天下國家盡人也既知所
以治人則積小高大而一變有至道之機由邇
可遠而四國有洽德之美自天下而言則遠人
也諸侯也吾皆有以曲成之而不遺自國家而
言則庶民也百工也臣也親也吾皆有以順施
之而各當矣不知所以治天下國家乎夫至於
治天下國家則文武之政行矣而其本則自脩
身始其機易決而其化至神君何憚而不爲耶
抑夫子作春秋以尊周爲本而此告哀公則勸
===
以治天下國家若王魯者何耶蓋春秋立君臣
之義以定萬世之經故其辭嚴而告哀公則微
視天命人心之去留向背以徇一時之權故其
辭婉要之平王東遷王迹已熄而天下漸不可
爲矣孔子之告哀公亦孟子勸齊梁之意也吾
於是又知孔孟之心則同
孟施舍之守氣又不如曾子之守約也
鄢懋卿
同考試官教諭李 批 守約處能盡說孟舍曾子
punctuated:
□人之稱，對已也。天下國家，盡人也。既知所以治人，則積小高大，而一變有至道之機；由邇可遠，而四國有洽德之美。自天下而言，則遠人也，諸侯也，吾皆有以曲成之而不遺；自國家而言，則庶民也，百工也，臣也，親也，吾皆有以順施之而各當矣。不知所以治天下國家乎？夫至於治天下國家，則文武之政行矣，而其本則自脩身始。其機易決，而其化至神，君何憚而不爲耶？抑夫子作《春秋》，以尊周爲本，而此告哀公，則勸以治天下國家，若王魯者，何耶？蓋《春秋》立君臣之義，以定萬世之經，故其辭嚴；而告哀公則微，視天命人心之去留向背，以徇一時之權，故其辭婉。要之，平王東遷，王迹已熄，而天下漸不可爲矣。孔子之告哀公，亦孟子勸齊梁之意也。吾於是又知孔孟之心則同。

孟施舍之守氣，又不如曾子之守約也。
鄢懋卿

同考試官教諭李批：守約處，能盡說孟舍、曾子
translation_en:
…[Illegible character] The term “others” stands in contrast to oneself. All under Heaven, the state, and the family consist entirely of people. Once one understands how to govern people, small achievements accumulate into great heights, and a single transformation offers the possibility of reaching the Way. From what is near one can reach what is distant, and the lands of the four quarters enjoy the beauty of virtue spreading everywhere. Speaking of all under Heaven, there are people from afar and the regional lords: I have the means to bring each to fulfillment according to their circumstances, overlooking none. Speaking of the state and family, there are the common people, the various artisans, ministers, and relatives: I have the means to deal with each appropriately, so that all receive their due. Would one then not understand how to govern all under Heaven, the state, and the family? When these are governed, the government of Kings Wen and Wu is put into practice; yet its foundation begins with cultivating oneself. The decisive step is readily taken, while its transforming influence is wondrous indeed. What should a ruler fear that would keep him from acting?

Yet when the Master composed the Spring and Autumn Annals, he took honoring the Zhou dynasty as his foundation. Here, however, in addressing Duke Ai, he urges him to govern all under Heaven, the state, and the family, as though making Lu a royal realm. Why is this? The Spring and Autumn Annals establishes the proper relationship between ruler and minister to fix an enduring norm for all ages; hence its language is stern. His words to Duke Ai, however, are subtle. He considers whether Heaven’s mandate and the people’s allegiance depart or remain, turn toward a ruler or turn away, and accommodates the expedient judgment required by the circumstances of the time; hence his language is gentle. Ultimately, after King Ping moved the capital eastward, the traces of true kingship had already vanished, and affairs under Heaven were gradually becoming impossible to remedy. Confucius’s words to Duke Ai have the same intent as Mencius’s exhortations to the rulers of Qi and Liang. From this I further understand that the hearts of Confucius and Mencius were alike.

“Meng Shishe’s maintaining his vital force, moreover, was inferior to Zengzi’s holding fast to the essential.”
Yan Maoqing.

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
之心殆遂於理學者
同考試官敎諭王　批　〔以守氣守約合此而作愈出愈深非淺學所及〕
同考試官敎諭孫　批　〔氣充才贍沛然不窮可式〕
考試官敎諭葉　批　〔是亦學而知要者矣〕
考試官敎授伍　批　〔講守約處甚精詳〕
大賢斷前人之勇主於理者大於氣也夫君子
靜定之學一理以爲之本也然則曾子義理之
勇豈孟舍血氣之可及哉孟子因論不動心之
===
有道而歸於曾子若謂語其槩則隨所執皆足
以不動心而要其極則非執之當者不足以語
不動心之至也是故勝不懼不勝亦不懼此孟
舍之所守以不動心者矣縮則往不縮則不往
此曾子之所守以不動心者矣然觀舍之把持
於進會之餘而卓然三軍之不畏者直守彼之
氣耳未必其理之果縮而可恃以無畏也若夫
會之量度於縮不縮之間而毅然萬人之亦往
者則守吾之理也理縮則氣可壯又烏計乎衆
punctuated:
之心，殆遂於理學者。

同考試官敎諭王，批：〔以守氣守約合此而作，愈出愈深，非淺學所及。〕

同考試官敎諭孫，批：〔氣充才贍，沛然不窮，可式。〕

考試官敎諭葉，批：〔是亦學而知要者矣。〕

考試官敎授伍，批：〔講守約處甚精詳。〕

大賢斷前人之勇，主於理者大於氣也。夫君子靜定之學，一理以爲之本也。然則曾子義理之勇，豈孟舍血氣之可及哉？孟子因論不動心之有道，而歸於曾子，若謂語其槩，則隨所執皆足以不動心；而要其極，則非執之當者，不足以語不動心之至也。是故勝不懼，不勝亦不懼，此孟舍之所守以不動心者矣；縮則往，不縮則不往，此曾子之所守以不動心者矣。然觀舍之把持於進會之餘，而卓然三軍之不畏者，直守彼之氣耳，未必其理之果縮，而可恃以無畏也。若夫會之量度於縮不縮之間，而毅然萬人之亦往者，則守吾之理也。理縮則氣可壯，又烏計乎衆
translation_en:
…their minds; the author is evidently well versed in the learning of principle [?].

Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔By bringing together maintaining one's vital force and holding to the essentials in treating this passage, the essay develops ever greater depth, beyond the reach of shallow learning.〕

Associate Examiner Sun, Instructor, comments: 〔Full of vigor and rich in talent, it flows abundantly without exhaustion. It may serve as a model.〕

Examiner Ye, Instructor, comments: 〔Here too is someone who has learned and understands what is essential.〕

Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: 〔The explanation of holding to the essentials is exceptionally precise and detailed.〕

The great worthy judged the courage of his predecessors: courage governed by principle surpasses courage grounded in vital force. The gentleman's learning of stillness and steadfastness takes principle alone as its foundation. How, then, could the physical courage of Meng She approach Zengzi's courage grounded in moral principle? In discussing the ways of keeping the mind unmoved, Mencius ultimately turned to Zengzi. It is as though he were saying that, broadly speaking, whatever one holds fast to may suffice to keep the mind unmoved; but to attain its utmost perfection, unless what one holds fast to is right, one cannot speak of the highest degree of an unmoved mind.

Thus, to be unafraid when victorious and equally unafraid when defeated was what Meng She held to in keeping his mind unmoved. To advance when in the right, and refrain from advancing when not in the right, was what Zengzi held to in keeping his mind unmoved. Yet observe how She maintained his resolve in advancing or withdrawing [?], standing firm without fear of the armies: he was merely maintaining his vital force. His position was not necessarily truly right in principle, such that he could rely upon it to remain fearless. As for Zengzi [?], who weighed whether he was in the right and resolutely advanced even against ten thousand men, he held fast to the principle within himself. When one is right in principle, one's vital force can be strong; why, then, reckon with the multitude …

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
眾之不敵哉故以舍比黝吾固以爲舍之守約
矣若以曾比舍吾又以爲曾之守約焉何也蓋
氣雖不可以不守然無理以主之則氣易窮惟
以理而御乎氣則氣之行也無往不利故自舍
言之曰能無懼也然所處不當自爾震蘇即使
隱忍以制終索然而不寧也以曾言之若不量
力也然內省不疚夫何憂懼即使不幸而敗亦
脫然無所悔也是舍之不動者猶有時而動也
而曾之不動者則無時而動也然則孟舍雖似
===
===
曾子又豈得於曾子班乎特以比於黝焉彼善
於此矣孟子之不動心其原蓋出於此故知言
所以明理養氣所以聚理其當大任而不動心
誠自以爲守約不殊於曾子也彼告子者雖曰
外義强制以幸不動心之名而充其類不免施
舍之守氣耳皆不足以語聖賢之道也嗚呼舍
之不得爲曾子固也告子學於孟子而不免焉
可惜也已
易

8. 脫然無所悔也是舍之不動者猶有時而動也

1. 曾子又豈得於曾子班乎特以比於黜爲彼善

家之不敵哉故以舍比黜吾固以爲舍之守約
矣若以曾比舍吾又以爲曾之守約焉何也蓋
氣雖不可以不守然無理以主之則氣易窮惟
以理而御乎氣則氣之行也無往不利故自舍
言之曰能無懼也然所慮不當自爾震蘇即使
隱忍以制終索然而不寧也以曾言之若不量
力也然內省不疚夫何憂懼即使不幸而敗亦
脫然無所悔也是舍之不動者猶有時而動也
而曾之不動者則無時而動也然則孟舍雖似
===
曾子又豈得於曾子班乎特以比於黜爲彼善
於此矣孟子之不動心其原蓋出於此故知言
所以明理養氣所以聚理其當大任而不動心
誠自以爲守約不殊於曾子也彼告子者雖曰
外義強制以幸不動心之名而究其類不免施
舍之守氣耳豈不足以語聖賢之道也嗚呼舍
之不得爲曾子固也告子學於孟子而不免焉
可惜也已
易
punctuated:
眾之不敵哉？故以舍比黝，吾固以爲舍之守約矣；若以曾比舍，吾又以爲曾之守約焉。何也？蓋氣雖不可以不守，然無理以主之，則氣易窮；惟以理而御乎氣，則氣之行也無往不利。故自舍言之，曰能無懼也，然所處不當，自爾震蘇，即使隱忍以制，終索然而不寧也。以曾言之，若不量力也，然內省不疚，夫何憂懼？即使不幸而敗，亦脫然無所悔也。是舍之不動者，猶有時而動也；而曾之不動者，則無時而動也。然則孟舍雖似曾子，又豈得於曾子班乎？特以比於黝焉，彼善於此矣。孟子之不動心，其原蓋出於此。故知言所以明理，養氣所以聚理，其當大任而不動心，誠自以爲守約不殊於曾子也。彼告子者，雖曰外義强制，以幸不動心之名，而充其類，不免施舍之守氣耳，皆不足以語聖賢之道也。嗚呼！舍之不得爲曾子，固也；告子學於孟子而不免焉，可惜也已！

易
translation_en:
…whether one is outmatched in numbers? Thus, comparing Meng Shishe with Beigong You, I certainly consider Shishe to have held to what is essential; but comparing Zengzi with Shishe, I consider Zengzi to have held to what is essential. Why? Although one cannot neglect to maintain one’s vital energy (qi), without principle to govern it that energy is easily exhausted. Only when principle directs vital energy can its operation succeed wherever it goes. Thus, speaking of Shishe, one may say that he was capable of fearlessness. Yet if his position were improper, he would naturally tremble with apprehension [?]; even if he restrained himself through silent endurance, he would ultimately remain dispirited and uneasy. Speaking of Zengzi, he might seem not to have measured his own strength. Yet if self-examination reveals no cause for shame, what is there to worry about or fear? Even if he were unfortunate enough to suffer defeat, he would remain free of regret. Thus Shishe’s unperturbed state could still at times be disturbed, whereas Zengzi’s could never be disturbed. Although Meng Shishe resembled Zengzi, then, how could he rank alongside him? It is only in comparison with Beigong You that the former was better than the latter.

The source of Mengzi’s unperturbed mind lay, it would seem, in this. Understanding words serves to clarify principle; nourishing vital energy serves to accumulate principle. In remaining unperturbed when shouldering great responsibilities, he truly considered his grasp of the essential no different from Zengzi’s. As for Gaozi, although he treated righteousness as external and imposed forcible restraint in hopes of attaining the reputation of an unperturbed mind, carrying his approach to its fullest extent would still leave him merely maintaining vital energy, like Shishe. Neither approach suffices for discussing the Way of the sages and worthies. Alas! That Shishe could not equal Zengzi is understandable; but that Gaozi, having studied under Mengzi, could not escape this limitation is regrettable indeed!

Book of Changes

易傳本益之卦德具爲學之大益焉蓋益長裕
而不設者也動巽兼資以爲學而學斯日進矣
其益也不亦大乎易傳廣益之義如此今夫學
問之道固所以求益於得而夫人之學毋病其

translation_en:
“Increase: through activity and yielding compliance, one advances daily without limit.”

Xiong Mingchen

Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “On a topic concerning the hexagram Increase, candidates find it very easy to produce an essay. Yet, on close consideration, most such writing is merely rambling verbiage. When an essay conveys the import of principle as coherently and harmoniously as this one, how could the examiners fail to regard its author with new respect?”

Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: “Its understanding of principle is precise and thorough, and its language harmonious and integrated. Here is a scholar who seeks improvement.”

Associate Examiner Sun, Instructor, comments: “Activity and yielding compliance support one another: they form a single undertaking. Writers often treat them in a fragmented way, so this essay has been selected as a model.”

Examiner Ye, Instructor, comments: “The understanding of the two terms ‘activity’ and ‘yielding compliance’ is genuine and exact. The following passage comes close to the ideal [?].”

Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: “The argument founded on turning toward goodness and correcting faults is most sound. The conclusion is especially rich in meaning.”

The Commentary on the Changes takes the virtues of the hexagram Increase as its basis and fully sets forth the great benefit they bring to learning. Increase means growth and abundance without restriction [?]. When activity and yielding compliance jointly support learning, learning advances daily. Is this not a great benefit indeed? Such is how the Commentary on the Changes expands upon the meaning of Increase. Now, the way of learning is certainly a means of seeking to increase what one has attained; yet people’s learning suffers from their failure to seek improvement properly [?]. Thus, those impatient to accomplish something sometimes stop when they encounter failure: this is not activity. Those who turn aside [?]…

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
□而施者或失則易非巽也是卦下體震也而
其德爲動上體巽也而其德爲巽則是自强不
息志不安於小成循序有常學惟欲其自得見
善則遷其行果矣而必寬裕以居之所謂勿忘
勿助者也有過則改自治勇矣而必優游以養
之所謂遜志時敏者也夫然學其不日進哉蓋
學之不進與進而不繼以无其機也自强不息
則上達之機存焉矣亦以无其漸也循序有常
則深造之漸存焉矣將見善之遷者由勉以至
===
於安積小高大而天德位焉王道行焉其爲學
也與日而俱進者也夫豈有彊乎過之改者由
寡以至於无厭脩乃來而盛德成焉大業出焉
其爲進也與日而俱邁者也又奚有彊乎學至
於是信乎其益之大矣吁此動而巽所以爲益
也雖然動巽以進學宜矣乃若艮則止之義也
大畜於艮亦以日新其德者之何歟蓋動巽君
子進脩之功也艮止聖人主靜立極之事也然
主靜非可以空寂求之則動巽者固其資耳學
punctuated: □而施者，或失則易，非巽也。是卦下體震也，而其德爲動；上體巽也，而其德爲巽。則是自强不息，志不安於小成；循序有常，學惟欲其自得。見善則遷，其行果矣，而必寬裕以居之，所謂勿忘勿助者也；有過則改，自治勇矣，而必優游以養之，所謂遜志時敏者也。夫然，學其不日進哉？蓋學之不進，與進而不繼，以无其機也；自强不息，則上達之機存焉矣。亦以无其漸也；循序有常，則深造之漸存焉矣。將見善之遷者，由勉以至於安，積小高大，而天德位焉，王道行焉。其爲學也，與日而俱進者也，夫豈有彊乎？過之改者，由寡以至於无，厭脩乃來，而盛德成焉，大業出焉。其爲進也，與日而俱邁者也，又奚有彊乎？學至於是，信乎其益之大矣！吁！此動而巽所以爲益也。雖然，動巽以進學宜矣，乃若艮，則止之義也，大畜於艮亦以日新其德者之何歟？蓋動巽，君子進脩之功也；艮止，聖人主靜立極之事也。然主靜非可以空寂求之，則動巽者固其資耳。學
translation_en:
…those who put it into practice in a □ manner [?], but change course upon a setback, are not truly yielding. In this hexagram, the lower trigram is Zhen, whose virtue is movement; the upper trigram is Xun, whose virtue is yielding. Thus one strengthens oneself unceasingly, one's aspirations never resting content with small achievements; one follows a constant sequence, seeking in learning only to attain understanding for oneself. On seeing goodness, one turns toward it: one's conduct is resolute, yet one must abide in it with breadth and ease. This is what is meant by neither forgetting nor trying to force growth. On having a fault, one corrects it: one is courageous in governing oneself, yet one must nurture oneself with calm and ease. This is what is meant by humility of purpose and continual diligence. With this, how could learning fail to advance daily?

Learning fails to advance, or advances without continuing, because it lacks an impulse. Through unceasing self-strengthening, the impulse toward higher understanding is preserved. It also fails because it lacks gradual progression. By consistently following the proper sequence, the gradual progression toward profound attainment is preserved. We shall then see those who turn toward goodness proceed from effort to ease, accumulating small gains into lofty and great attainments, so that heavenly virtue becomes established and the kingly Way is put into practice. Their learning advances with each passing day: how could it have any limit? Those who correct their faults proceed from having few to having none; further cultivation then comes [?], so that abundant virtue is perfected and great undertakings emerge. Their progress keeps pace with each passing day: what limit could it have? When learning reaches this point, its increase is indeed great! Ah! This is why movement combined with yielding constitutes Increase.

Nevertheless, while movement and yielding are fitting means of advancing learning, Gen signifies stopping. How is it, then, that in Great Accumulation, Gen likewise serves to renew one's virtue daily? Movement and yielding are the work by which the gentleman advances in self-cultivation; the stillness of Gen is the work by which the sage gives primacy to tranquility and establishes the ultimate standard. Yet this primacy of tranquility cannot be sought through emptiness and quiescence; movement and yielding are assuredly its resources. Those who learn…

…those who study should [not] regard them differently.

“Those who know the way of change and transformation—surely they know what the numinous does!”

Shao Kuiming

Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: 〔Change and transformation and the numinous are not two separate things. Knowing change and transformation means knowing the numinous. This composition grasps that.〕

Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔The reasoning has no gaps, and the wording is carefully weighed. The author is accomplished in the Changes [?].〕

The Great Commentary considers the numerical procedures of the Changes and deeply marvels at their subtlety. How profound it is that the changes and transformations of these numerical procedures are all the work of the numinous! To know change and transformation is to know the numinous. No wonder the sage brings out their subtlety and marvels at it! His meaning, moreover, is that the Changes has numbers and procedures, all of which constitute the way of change and transformation. title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
□以□識其機於揲著求卦之法而凡陰□
□進退離合者皆有以潛會其用不徒觀數
之文而已因數考變而得意以忘言謂圖具天
地之數可也謂吾心即圖之精亦可也蓋有得
於形器之外者矣不徒究卦之迹而已假象明
理而極深以研幾謂法洩天地之秘可也謂吾
心即法之靈亦可也蓋有契於言意之表者矣
若然則知數之有變化也孰主張是要皆莫之
爲而自爲者人之心思固有所不遍焉法之有
變化也孰綱維是要皆莫之致而自致者人之
===
智力則亦无所容焉故人徒知夫數法之原夫
地開之也而不知天地者能開其端而不能必
其成至於曲成之妙天地亦不得而專也又徒
知夫數法之衍聖人制之也而不知聖人者能
成其能而不能强其合至於會合之妙聖人亦
不得而與也噫其殆天下之至神者乎是故知
變化之道者則知神之所爲矣竊嘗疑之神者
不可知之謂也今而曰知神之爲何哉□
punctuated: □以□識其機，於揲著求卦之法，而凡陰□□進退離合者，皆有以潛會其用。不徒觀數之文而已，因數考變，而得意以忘言，謂圖具天地之數可也，謂吾心即圖之精亦可也，蓋有得於形器之外者矣。不徒究卦之迹而已，假象明理，而極深以研幾，謂法洩天地之秘可也，謂吾心即法之靈亦可也，蓋有契於言意之表者矣。若然，則知數之有變化也，孰主張是？要皆莫之爲而自爲者，人之心思固有所不遍焉。法之有變化也，孰綱維是？要皆莫之致而自致者，人之智力則亦无所容焉。故人徒知夫數法之原，夫地開之也，而不知天地者能開其端而不能必其成；至於曲成之妙，天地亦不得而專也。又徒知夫數法之衍，聖人制之也，而不知聖人者能成其能而不能强其合；至於會合之妙，聖人亦不得而與也。噫！其殆天下之至神者乎！是故知變化之道者，則知神之所爲矣。竊嘗疑之：神者，不可知之謂也，今而曰知神之爲，何哉？□
translation_en:
…[?] discern their workings; and, in the method of manipulating yarrow stalks [?] to obtain hexagrams, inwardly apprehend the operation of all the advancing and retreating, separating and joining of yin [illegible]. One does not merely observe the outward patterns of the numbers: through the numbers one examines change, grasps the meaning, and forgets the words. One may say that the Diagram contains the numbers of Heaven and Earth; one may also say that one’s own mind is the very essence of the Diagram. For one has attained something beyond material forms and objects. Nor does one merely investigate the traces of the hexagrams: through images one illuminates principle, plumbing the depths to investigate the incipient workings of things. One may say that the method discloses the secrets of Heaven and Earth; one may also say that one’s own mind is the very numinous efficacy of the method. For one has apprehended something beyond words and meanings.

If this is so, then, knowing that numbers undergo change and transformation, one asks: who governs this? In essence, all of it happens of itself, without anyone making it happen; human thought certainly cannot encompass it all. Who orders the changes and transformations of the method? In essence, all of them come about of themselves, without anyone bringing them about; human intellect and effort likewise have no place in them. Thus people know only that the origin of the numbers and method was opened up by earth [?]. They do not know that Heaven and Earth can initiate them but cannot ensure their completion; as for the wondrous efficacy by which each thing is brought to fulfillment in all its particulars, even Heaven and Earth cannot claim sole command of it. Again, people know only that the elaboration of the numbers and method was fashioned by the sages. They do not know that the sages can bring their capacities to fulfillment but cannot force their concordance; as for the wondrous efficacy of their coming together in accord, even the sages cannot intervene in it. Ah! Is this not perhaps the utmost numinous power under Heaven? Thus those who know the Way of change and transformation know what numinous power does.

I have privately wondered about this: the numinous is what is called unknowable. Why, then, speak now of knowing what numinous power does? [Illegible]…

欲在仁也人君因而育之天下有不歸心者鮮
矣安民之功用如是大臣以語同列所以勵其
君也蓋謂天下之治忽繫民心民心之萃渙在
punctuated:

translation_en:
…This does not mean that the numinous can be known. It merely speaks profoundly of the subtlety of numerical methods, regarding it as the □ of the numinous [?], to make it manifest to all under Heaven and to later generations. What, then, should we do? The Book of Changes says: “Making it numinous and illuminating it depends upon the person; silently accomplishing it and securing trust without words depends upon one's virtuous conduct.” Virtuous conduct is the Changes within the heart. Only after grasping the Changes within the heart can one discuss the Changes. As for those who imitated the Changes in the Supreme Mystery (Taixuan) and the Hidden Void (Qianxu), did they truly understand the Changes?

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
君德故爲治者惠民不安耳誠能容保無疆合
羣生而長養之使各迪于吉康教思無窮舉一
世而甄陶之使各正其性命安民如是則是仁
足以長人德之出于身者無不漸被何異於乾
之以美利利天下乎愛足以濟衆澤之加于民
者無不淪洽何異於坤之以厚德載物乎是則
所謂惠矣夫惠固無心之感也然君以民爲心
則民必以君爲心自愛戴而歸往仁特君之自
盡耳然慎厥麗乃勸則民亦惟刑用勸自仰慕
===
而悅服若干政者遂所欲而懷其恩樂樂利利
蓋有沒世不能忘者矣化于訓者全所性而懷
其德尊尊親親蓋有固結不可解者矣是則安
民而至於民懷則仁之功用著矣況知其官人
而兼盡之其可以易而爲乎抑孔子之賛舜曰
無爲而治者其舜也與則治又若易易焉者何
耶蓋君天也天運於上而四時行百物生易簡
而已矣人君任相相舉賢才天下之民不勞而
治者法天而已矣故孟子曰舜以不得禹臯陶
punctuated: 君德。故爲治者惠民不安耳。誠能容保無疆，合羣生而長養之，使各迪于吉康；教思無窮，舉一世而甄陶之，使各正其性命。安民如是，則是仁足以長人，德之出于身者無不漸被，何異於乾之以美利利天下乎？愛足以濟衆，澤之加于民者無不淪洽，何異於坤之以厚德載物乎？是則所謂惠矣。夫惠固無心之感也，然君以民爲心，則民必以君爲心，自愛戴而歸往。仁特君之自盡耳，然慎厥麗乃勸，則民亦惟刑用勸，自仰慕而悅服。若干政者遂所欲而懷其恩，樂樂利利，蓋有沒世不能忘者矣；化于訓者全所性而懷其德，尊尊親親，蓋有固結不可解者矣。是則安民而至於民懷，則仁之功用著矣。況知其官人而兼盡之，其可以易而爲乎？抑孔子之賛舜曰：「無爲而治者，其舜也與？」則治又若易易焉者，何耶？蓋君，天也。天運於上，而四時行、百物生，易簡而已矣。人君任相，相舉賢才，天下之民不勞而治者，法天而已矣。故孟子曰：「舜以不得禹臯陶
translation_en:
…the ruler’s virtue. Thus, those who govern bestow benefits upon the people but do not bring them peace [?]. If the ruler can truly embrace and protect without limit, gathering all living beings together and nurturing them so that each advances toward good fortune and well-being; if his concern for instruction is inexhaustible, molding an entire generation so that each realizes aright its nature and allotted destiny—if he brings peace to the people in this way, then his benevolence suffices to lead others. The virtue issuing from his person will gradually reach everywhere: how does this differ from Qian, Heaven, benefiting all under Heaven through its excellent bounty? His love suffices to succor the multitude, and the blessings he extends to the people penetrate everywhere: how does this differ from Kun, Earth, sustaining all things through its ample virtue? This, then, is what is called beneficence.

Beneficence indeed moves others without any deliberate intention to do so. Yet when the ruler takes the people’s concerns as his own, the people will surely take the ruler’s concerns as their own, naturally loving, supporting, and turning toward him. Benevolence is simply the ruler’s fulfillment of his own obligations. Yet, as the saying goes, “Be careful about what you attach yourself to, and you will be encouraged”; the people too will follow his example and thereby be encouraged, naturally admiring him and submitting gladly. Those affected by his government [?] attain what they desire and cherish his kindness, delighting in what brings them delight and benefiting from what benefits them; indeed, some will be unable to forget him to the end of their lives. Those transformed by his instruction fully realize their innate nature and cherish his virtue, honoring those worthy of honor and loving those who should be loved; indeed, their attachment becomes so firm that it cannot be dissolved. When bringing peace to the people thus leads them to cherish their ruler, the efficacy of benevolence becomes manifest.

Moreover, if he understands how to appoint men to office and fully accomplishes both tasks, can this be done with ease? Yet Confucius praised Shun, saying, “Was it not Shun who governed through nonaction?” Why, then, does governing again appear so very easy? The ruler is Heaven. Heaven moves above, the four seasons proceed, and the myriad things come into being: it is simply ease and simplicity. The ruler appoints chief ministers, and the chief ministers recommend worthy and talented men. That the people throughout the realm are governed without toil is simply a matter of modeling oneself on Heaven. Thus Mencius said, “Shun took not obtaining Yu and Gao Yao…

text:
□爲己憂焉與夫子之言相表裏然則知人安民
分之則二而要其歸則安民未有不本於知人
者君人者宜慎諸
凡人未見聖若不克見既見聖亦不克由
聖爾其戒哉爾惟風下民惟草

賢王欲大臣之由前訓必戒以常情而示以化
機也蓋上之於下其感應之機甚速也苟惟常
情之是狥焉則將率之而不從矣是可以不戒
哉昔成王命君陳尹茲東郊而告之如此若曰
我謂周公之訓所當由者以治至聖人而止論
治者亦惟以聖人爲宗耳但凡人之情重於所

Thus, discerning worthy men and bringing peace to the people are two tasks when considered separately; yet, considered in their ultimate purpose, bringing peace to the people invariably rests upon discerning worthy men. Those who rule others should attend carefully to this.

“Ordinary people, before they have seen a sage, act as though they might never succeed in seeing him; once they have seen a sage, they still fail to follow him. Be on your guard against this! You are the wind; the common people are the grass.”

Jiang Kun

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
間而輕於所見方其未見聖也則好德動於秉
彝之良而曰聖人吾不得而見矣慨慕之甚切
若弗克見焉及其既見聖也則私心奪於物欲
之蔽而曰聖人亦若是而已矣怠忽之隨生亦
弗克由焉是則人之情大抵然也爾之東郊必
戒之哉夫爾於周公則既嘗見之矣周公日擊
殷民之亂其操心甚危而慮患甚深也汝繼其
後必以周公之心爲心期於共濟而不必其法
自我立周公深惟東郊之治其爲謨甚訂而爲
===
猷甚遠也汝居其位必以周公之事爲事期於
相成而不必其功自已出所以然者何哉蓋爾
之於民以鼓舞爲德譬之在天其惟風也民之
於爾以順從爲德譬之在地其惟草也風行則
草偃而自有感應之孚上立則下從而自有神
化之妙故爾能由周公之訓以風乎民則民亦
以懷周公者而從乎爾其於化殷也又何難哉
雖然周公治殷以謹毖爲務成王欲君陳由訓
乃有取於寛和何邪蓋道有定體政無定用故
punctuated:
間而輕於所見。方其未見聖也，則好德動於秉彝之良，而曰：「聖人吾不得而見矣。」慨慕之甚切，若弗克見焉。及其既見聖也，則私心奪於物欲之蔽，而曰：「聖人亦若是而已矣。」怠忽之隨生，亦弗克由焉。是則人之情大抵然也。爾之東郊，必戒之哉！夫爾於周公，則既嘗見之矣。周公日擊殷民之亂，其操心甚危，而慮患甚深也。汝繼其後，必以周公之心爲心，期於共濟，而不必其法自我立。周公深惟東郊之治，其爲謨甚訂，而爲猷甚遠也。汝居其位，必以周公之事爲事，期於相成，而不必其功自已出。所以然者何哉？蓋爾之於民，以鼓舞爲德，譬之在天，其惟風也；民之於爾，以順從爲德，譬之在地，其惟草也。風行則草偃，而自有感應之孚；上立則下從，而自有神化之妙。故爾能由周公之訓以風乎民，則民亦以懷周公者而從乎爾。其於化殷也，又何難哉？

雖然，周公治殷以謹毖爲務，成王欲君陳由訓，乃有取於寛和，何邪？蓋道有定體，政無定用，故
translation_en:
…what they have heard [?], while slighting what they have seen. Before they have seen a sage, their love of virtue springs from the goodness of their innate moral nature, and they say, “A sage—I cannot obtain the chance to see one!” Their longing and admiration are intensely earnest, as though they might never succeed in seeing him. Once they have seen a sage, however, selfish impulses take over as material desires obscure their understanding, and they say, “A sage is merely like this.” Indifference and neglect then arise, and they prove unable to follow him. Such, broadly speaking, are human feelings. When you go to the eastern suburbs, you must guard against this!

As for Zhou Gong, you have already seen him yourself. Zhou Gong daily combated disorder among the people of Yin [?]; his mind was deeply apprehensive, and his concern for possible troubles was profound. Succeeding him, you must take his concerns as your own, aiming to bring the undertaking to completion together, without insisting that its rules originate with you. Zhou Gong pondered deeply the governance of the eastern suburbs; his plans were carefully settled [?], and his designs reached far into the future. Occupying his position, you must take his work as your own, aiming to bring it to fulfillment, without insisting that the achievement be yours alone. Why is this so? Your virtue toward the people consists in stirring and inspiring them: among things in heaven, you are like the wind. The people’s virtue toward you consists in willing obedience: among things on earth, they are like the grass. When the wind blows, the grass bends; influence and response naturally correspond with unfailing fidelity. When those above establish an example, those below follow; therein naturally lies the wondrous efficacy of spiritual transformation. Thus, if you can follow Zhou Gong’s instructions and thereby influence the people, they too will follow you with the same affection they cherish for Zhou Gong. What difficulty, then, could there be in transforming the people of Yin?

Nevertheless, Zhou Gong made vigilance and caution his chief concern in governing Yin. Why, then, did King Cheng favor generosity and harmony when he wished Jun Chen to follow those instructions? The Way has a constant substance, but government has no fixed application; therefore …

必通其變使民不倦神而化之使民宜之然後
明德之治日新而馨香之感格益至若曰由周
公之訓而尚泥於謹始之迹則非所以由周公
之心矣此又論由訓者所當知

詩人美王者本繼先之孝而周作室之用焉夫

詩人美王者本繼先之孝，而周作室之用焉。夫興作，國家所重也。王者周作室之用，而本諸繼先之孝，其斯為可美歟？詩人於落成之際歌之。
translation_en:
…One must adapt to changing circumstances so that the people do not grow weary, transforming them with wondrous efficacy so that they find it fitting. Only then will government through illustrious virtue be renewed daily, and its fragrant influence reach ever more fully to the spirits. If one claims to follow the Duke of Zhou’s instructions yet remains bound to the outward practices of his initial caution, this is no way to follow the Duke of Zhou’s true intent. This, too, is something those who discuss following his instructions ought to understand.

Book of Odes
“Continuing the ancestral mothers and forefathers, he built a dwelling with a hundred wall-sections, its doors facing west and south. Here he dwells, here he rests; here he laughs, here he speaks.”
Zhang Xiju
Associate Examiner Deng, an Instructor, comments: “Closely reasoned and thoughtfully conceived.”
Associate Examiner Tang, an Instructor, comments: “Upright and grand, with creative force; an exposition of the meaning of the Elegantiae should be like this.”
Associate Examiner Xu, an Instructor, comments: “This □ places the emphasis on carrying on the forebears’ work, with an insight uniquely his own [?].”

Examiner Wu, a Professor, comments: “Dignified and refined.”

The poet praises the king for grounding his provision of all that a dwelling requires in the filial devotion that carries on the work of his forebears. Building projects are indeed matters of great importance to the state. When a king provides fully for the uses of a dwelling and grounds this in filial devotion to his forebears, is this not worthy of praise? The poet sang of it at the time of its completion…

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
如此意謂天子以四海爲家而聖人以繼述爲
孝昔周中葉王靈嘗不振矣王居嘗不守矣維宣
王克修攘之功樹中興之業知夫宅中圖大姬
祖之經營以垂裕者甚備也而不敢使耿光之
弗墜又念夫居重馭輕姬祖之締造以貽後者
甚艱也而必期於大烈之對揚勞非所憚也身
任夫堂構之責而若或臨之凡謀爲於今者固
將以似其事焉費非所惜也志專於菟塈之圖
而若或見之凡興作於今者罔非以續其緒焉
===
是故乃召司空乃召司徒則絡勾陳以繚垣而
翼翼然百堵之在望矣考諸中星揆諸日景則闢
閶闔以啓扉而翚然西南之錯見矣於是居且
處焉所謂當宁而朝當依而覲者此也所謂路
寢聽政小寢釋服者此也而其景象不有以新
天下之耳目乎於是笑且語焉以睦九族以親
諸侯以樂嘉賓者此也以圖人事以陳衆謨以
協群慮者此也而其氣勢不有以繫天下之心
志乎故曰匪棘其欲遹追來孝信宣王之能中
punctuated:
如此。意謂天子以四海爲家，而聖人以繼述爲孝。昔周中葉，王靈嘗不振矣，王居嘗不守矣。維宣王克修攘之功，樹中興之業，知夫宅中圖大，姬祖之經營以垂裕者甚備也，而不敢使耿光之弗墜；又念夫居重馭輕，姬祖之締造以貽後者甚艱也，而必期於大烈之對揚。勞非所憚也，身任夫堂構之責，而若或臨之，凡謀爲於今者，固將以似其事焉；費非所惜也，志專於菟塈之圖，而若或見之，凡興作於今者，罔非以續其緒焉。
是故乃召司空，乃召司徒，則絡勾陳以繚垣，而翼翼然百堵之在望矣；考諸中星，揆諸日景，則闢閶闔以啓扉，而翚然西南之錯見矣。於是居且處焉，所謂當宁而朝、當依而覲者，此也；所謂路寢聽政、小寢釋服者，此也。而其景象不有以新天下之耳目乎？於是笑且語焉，以睦九族、以親諸侯、以樂嘉賓者，此也；以圖人事、以陳衆謨、以協群慮者，此也。而其氣勢不有以繫天下之心志乎？故曰：「匪棘其欲，遹追來孝。」信宣王之能中
translation_en:
…thus. The meaning is that the Son of Heaven takes all within the Four Seas as his home, while the sage regards carrying forward his predecessors’ undertakings as filial piety. In the middle period of the Zhou, royal prestige had faltered, and the royal residence had ceased to be secure. King Xuan accomplished the work of restoring order and repelling enemies, establishing the achievement of a dynastic restoration. He understood that, in occupying the center and planning for greatness, the ancestors of the Ji house had made most thorough arrangements to bequeath prosperity; he therefore dared not allow their brilliant glory to remain undiminished [?]. He also reflected that, in occupying the commanding center and controlling the subordinate regions, those ancestors had endured great hardship in laying foundations for their descendants; he therefore resolved to honor and carry forward their great achievements. He did not shrink from toil: personally assuming responsibility for completing his forebears’ building, he acted as though someone stood over him. Whatever he planned and undertook in the present was intended to emulate their deeds. Nor did he begrudge expense: intent upon plans for thatching and plastering [?], he acted as though someone watched him. Every construction undertaken in the present continued the work they had begun.
Thus he summoned the Minister of Works and summoned the Minister of Education. Walls encircled the palace precinct, and a hundred stately stretches of wall came into view. He consulted the stars at their meridian transit and measured the sun’s shadow; then the palace gates were opened and their doors thrown wide, while structures resembling pheasants in flight appeared here and there to the west and south. Here he dwelt and remained. This was the place meant by standing in the court to hold audience and standing before the screen to receive those paying court; this was the place meant by hearing affairs of government in the principal chamber and removing ceremonial robes in the lesser chamber. Did not this sight renew the eyes and ears of all under Heaven? Here he laughed and conversed. This was where he brought harmony to the nine degrees of kinship, drew the feudal lords close, and gave pleasure to honored guests; this was where human affairs were considered, the many counsels presented, and everyone’s deliberations brought into accord. Did not its commanding presence bind the hearts and aspirations of all under Heaven? Thus it is said: “He did not hasten to gratify his desires, but pursued the filial devotion handed down to him.” Truly, King Xuan was able to bring about a restoration…

translation_en:
…revive the dynasty. Even so, this merely magnifies the splendor of a particular moment. Its foundation lies elsewhere. In humbling himself and cultivating his conduct, did he not feel the anxiety expressed in “The Milky Way” (Yunhan)? In attending court early and retiring late, did he not ask, “How far has the night advanced?” Thus, the palace celebrated in “The Si Stream” (Sigan) constitutes a true accomplishment when accompanied by government like King Xuan’s. Without King Xuan’s government, it amounts in the end merely to the building of a thousand gates and ten thousand doors in later ages. Those who discuss building projects should distinguish these things.

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
□□人也有以其此祀高宗之樂歌叙其既克
□□而告之之言曰天立君也所以爲華夷之主
□故天下之政必出於一而不可以今昔言天
下之人必歸於一而不可以遠近論嗟女荆楚
阻洞庭彭蠡以爲雄自以爲居則遠矣然依五
服九州以立國實在乎亳之南焉封疆伊邇聲
教所加風土不殊正朔必及其與我商之臣僕
也而今何如哉不聞我商之成湯將乎由盤庚而
上則有成湯爲之君中間太甲太戊之統承無
===
論已自荆楚而西亦有氐羌爲之國近而常顧
昆吾之率服無論已是故時必以享實服之制
也而彼則不敢以數而不恭凡所以脩庭實而
將問者靡或遠也終必以王賓服之制也而彼
則不敢以遠而遂廢凡所以執玉帛而稱臣者
無敢懈也則曰茲享也非今作也自受命以
來未之有改也且吾聞先王之訓不享者有征
討之備而又奚後焉亦曰茲王也非自茲始也

translation_en:
…[illegible] people [?]. In this sacrificial hymn to Gaozong, someone recounts the words addressed to them after he had conquered [illegible], saying: “Heaven establishes a ruler to be lord of both the Chinese and the peoples beyond them. [Illegible] Thus government throughout the world must issue from a single authority; no distinction can be made between present and past. All the people of the world must submit to a single ruler; no distinction can be made between far and near.

“Ah, you people of Jingchu! Relying on Dongting and Pengli as barriers, you deem yourselves powerful and imagine that your dwelling lies far away. Yet, within the Five Zones of Submission and the Nine Regions, your state actually lies south of Bo. Your borders are so near that our civilizing influence reaches them; your customs and land are not so different that our calendar should fail to extend to you. You too are subjects and servants of our Shang: how, then, do matters stand today? Have you not heard of our Shang’s Cheng Tang [?]? Looking back from Pan Geng, there was Cheng Tang as ruler, to say nothing of the intervening succession of Tai Jia and Tai Wu. Westward from Jingchu there were also the states of the Di and Qiang, to say nothing of the submission of nearby Changgu [?] and Kunwu.

“Accordingly, they must present offerings at the appointed seasons: this is the system of submission through offerings [?]. They dare not become disrespectful because these duties recur frequently. None considers itself too distant to prepare the gifts displayed in the court and convey its greetings. At the end of a ruler’s lifetime, they must attend the royal court: this is the system governing the guest zone of submission. They dare not let distance become a reason to abandon the practice. None dares neglect bearing jade and silk and declaring itself a subject.

“Thus they say: ‘These offerings are no present innovation. Since the reception of Heaven’s Mandate, they have never been altered. Moreover, we have heard the instruction of the former kings: against those who do not present offerings, preparations are made for punitive expeditions. Moreover, we have heard the regulation of the former kings: those who do not…

title: 嘉靖十六年江西鄉試錄
text:
王者有文告之辭而又奚後焉是則與服於遠而
不服於近服於先王而不服於今日謂之常者
可乎彼戎而波不至我以是隣兵而來也亦求
以續其緒而已豈欲勤兵於遠哉吁不觀之兵
則爲不武不聲之罪則爲無名而高宗之師業
有之吾以是而知其中興之有自矣雖然窮兵
遠討老師費財皆兵家之所忌也而鬼方之伐
深入其阻三年而後克之不幾於犯厥忌乎而
終以克者何也孟子嘗言之矣由湯至於武丁
賢聖之君六七作蓋人之戴商也維舊而楚之
叛之也獨先此高宗所以不得已而興師也故
雖深入而不爲窮三年而不爲老卒亦未嘗不
直且壯也否則其不爲秦皇漢武之師也者幾
希
===
春秋
秋荆伐鄭公會齊人宋人救鄭〔莊公二十八年〕
〔僖公元年〕
衛人許人救鄭〔文公九年〕
楚人伐鄭公子遂會晉人宋人
punctuated:
王者有文告之辭，而又奚後焉？是則與服於遠而不服於近，服於先王而不服於今日，謂之常者可乎？彼戎而波不至，我以是隣兵而來也，亦求以續其緒而已，豈欲勤兵於遠哉？吁！不觀之兵，則爲不武；不聲之罪，則爲無名。而高宗之師業有之，吾以是而知其中興之有自矣。雖然，窮兵遠討，老師費財，皆兵家之所忌也。而鬼方之伐，深入其阻，三年而後克之，不幾於犯厥忌乎？而終以克者，何也？孟子嘗言之矣：「由湯至於武丁，賢聖之君六七作。」蓋人之戴商也維舊，而楚之叛之也獨先，此高宗所以不得已而興師也。故雖深入而不爲窮，三年而不爲老，卒亦未嘗不直且壯也。否則，其不爲秦皇漢武之師也者幾希。

衛人、許人救鄭。〔文公九年〕

translation_en:
…for those who fail to attend the king, there are formal proclamations of admonition. Why, then, should they lag behind? Could submission at a distance but refusal to submit nearby, or submission to the former kings but refusal to submit today, be called constancy? Those Rong failed to come [?], and we therefore came with troops [?], seeking only to carry on the established order. How could the intention have been to wear out armies in distant lands? Ah! Failing to display military force would show a lack of martial resolve; failing to proclaim their crimes would leave the campaign without a justifying cause. Gaozong’s army already possessed both. From this I understand that his restoration of the dynasty had a firm foundation.

Nevertheless, exhausting one’s forces on distant expeditions, wearing out armies, and wasting resources are all things that military strategists shun. Yet the campaign against Guifang penetrated deep into its difficult terrain, and victory came only after three years. Did this not verge on violating those very prohibitions? Why, then, did it ultimately succeed? Mengzi once said: “From Tang to Wuding, six or seven worthy and sagely rulers arose.” The people’s allegiance to Shang was thus longstanding, while Chu [?] alone took the lead in rebellion. This was why Gaozong had no choice but to raise an army. Thus, though his troops penetrated deeply, they were not exhausted; though the campaign lasted three years, they were not worn out. Throughout, their cause remained just and their strength vigorous. Otherwise, there would have been scarcely any difference between his army and those of the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of Han.

In autumn, Jing attacked Zheng. The duke joined men of Qi and Song to relieve Zheng. 〔Twenty-eighth year of Duke Zhuang〕〔First year of Duke Xi〕
Men of Wei and Xu relieved Zheng. 〔Ninth year of Duke Wen〕

When foreign troops first ravaged a state of divided allegiance, the hegemonic lord was diligent in relieving its distress; when foreign troops again ravaged that state, the minister concerned with its welfare [?] was negligent in relieving its distress. Thus diligence and negligence in hegemonic affairs bear upon the waxing and waning of the foreign peoples and the Central States. There is good reason for the attention that the Spring and Autumn Annals gives to its entries recording Jing and Chu attacking Zheng, and Qi and Jin rescuing Zheng!
In the closing years [?] of our Duke Zhuang’s reign, the beneficent influence of the royal house was already exhausted, and Chu’s power was gradually growing stronger. Although Duke Huan of Qi had begun to establish his hegemony and had ambitions concerning the regional lords, Chu did not yet fear him. Thereupon Chu took advantage [?] of Ziyuan’s campaign to pursue vengeance on account of a woman [?], deploying its forces to attack Zheng. Why was this? It was merely relying on its strength to intimidate the Central States. Was this not an army that feared the few [?]?

害之地楚欲得志於中國乃所必爭者也齊桓

不以爲急是以桓文之時伯業大盛靈成之際
punctuated: 公伯齊，本欲攘夷安夏者也。今主夏兵，而其勤畢□此，世道不有賴邪？故楚以州舉，狄之也；而於齊桓、魯、宋之救，特書以善之。非以桓爲勤，而見其主兵之實乎？我文中年，伯圖將衰，楚强於是乎日盛矣。況晉靈幼弱，不在諸侯，用宜爲其所輕也。於是楚穆用范山北方可圖之策，而遂親將以伐鄭焉。此何故哉？不過要其從以爭中國耳，非貪得之兵與？趙盾志不在此，徐率宋、衛諸國而救之。雖華耦、孔達皆國卿也，然而夷氣甚熾，尚有宴安之懷；鄰難方殷，不急簡書之畏。卒使楚師得利先還，而鄭人狠淵之平不及止焉。噫！趙盾相晉，本非折衝消患者也。既啓戎心，而其怠又如此，國事將誰託邪？故楚以人稱，貶之也；而於趙盾、華、孔之救，皆貶而人之。非以盾爲怠，而見其啓戎之罪乎？抑論鄭在當時，爲要害之地，楚欲得志於中國，乃所必爭者也。齊桓知此，故汲汲焉，惟鄭是圖；趙盾不知，故泄泄焉，不以爲急。是以桓、文之時，伯業大盛；靈、成之際，
translation_en:
…Duke Huan exercised hegemony from Qi, originally intending to repel the barbarians and secure the Chinese states. Now he commanded the forces of those states and displayed such diligence [?; one character illegible]: did not the order of the world depend upon him? Thus Chu is designated by its regional name, treating it as barbarian; the relief undertaken by Duke Huan of Qi, Lu, and Song is expressly recorded to commend it. Is this not to credit Huan with diligence and reveal how he actually fulfilled his command of the armies?

In the middle years of our Duke Wen [?], the enterprise of hegemony was approaching decline, while Chu’s strength grew daily. Moreover, Duke Ling of Jin was young and weak and held no standing among the regional lords [?], so it was natural that Chu should hold him in contempt. Duke Mu of Chu therefore adopted Fan Shan’s proposal that the north could be brought under his designs, and personally led an attack on Zheng. Why did he do this? It was merely to compel Zheng’s submission and contend for the central states. Was this not warfare driven by greed for gain? Zhao Dun’s purpose was not directed to this danger; he slowly led Song, Wei, and the other states to Zheng’s relief. Although Hua Ou and Kong Da were both ministers of their states, even as barbarian aggression blazed fiercely, they still cherished ease and repose. With their neighbor’s distress at its height, they felt no urgency at the obligations imposed by written summonses. In the end, they allowed Chu’s army to gain its advantage and withdraw first, and were too late to prevent the people of Zheng from making peace at Henyuan [?]. Alas! Zhao Dun, as chief minister of Jin, was never one to repel aggression and avert calamity. Having already emboldened the enemy, he was moreover so negligent: to whom could the affairs of the state be entrusted? Thus Chu’s commander is called merely a “man,” a demotion; in recording the relief undertaken by Zhao Dun, Hua Ou, and Kong Da, all are likewise demoted and called “men.” Is this not to condemn Dun’s negligence and reveal his culpability in encouraging aggression?

Consider further that Zheng at that time occupied a strategically crucial position. If Chu wished to realize its ambitions in the central states, Zheng was a place it had to contest. Duke Huan of Qi understood this, and so acted with urgency, making Zheng his sole concern. Zhao Dun did not understand it, and so remained indifferent, treating it as no urgent matter. Thus, in the time of Dukes Huan and Wen, hegemony flourished greatly; in the time of Dukes Ling and Cheng…
